title: "There Are Only Two Hard Problems in Computer Science"
subtitle: …cache invalidation, naming things, and off-by-one errors. The joke is famous because caching really is that treacherous — and that essential.
hook: There's an old programmer joke: 'There are only two hard things in computer science: cache invalidation and naming things.' It's funny because it's true. **Caching** — keeping a copy of something close so you don't fetch it the slow way twice — is everywhere and speeds up the whole digital world. But keeping those copies *correct* is one of the genuinely hard problems in the field. Today: why caching is both a superpower and a curse.

sections.heading: What a cache is
sections.body: A **cache** is a small, fast store holding copies of things that are expensive to fetch, so the next request is instant. Your CPU caches memory; your browser caches images; a **CDN** caches web pages on servers near you (that's why a viral video doesn't melt one origin server). The payoff is huge: turn a slow trip down the latency ladder into a fast local hit.

sections.heading: Why invalidation is hell
sections.body: Here's the rub: the original data can *change*. Now your fast copy is **stale** — confidently serving the old answer. So when do you throw the copy away and re-fetch? Too eager and you lose the speed benefit; too lazy and users see wrong, outdated data. There's no clean universal answer — it depends on how fresh the data must be, and getting it wrong causes some of the most confusing bugs there are ('but I updated it — why do I still see the old one?').

sections.caption: A cache hit is instant. But when the source changes, the cached copy is stale — and deciding when to invalidate it is the hard part.

sections.label: Common strategies
sections.body: Real systems tame it with rules: TTL (time-to-live — copy expires after N seconds), write-through (update the cache whenever you update the source), and explicit invalidation (tell the cache 'this changed'). Each trades freshness against speed and complexity. There's no free answer — only the right trade-off for how stale you can afford to be.

sections.caption: CDNs, caching, and cache invalidation — the whole picture in ~15 minutes.

takeaways: A **cache** keeps a fast local copy of expensive-to-fetch data (CPU, browser, CDN).
It converts a slow trip down the latency ladder into an instant local **hit**.
The hard part is **invalidation**: when the source changes, the copy goes **stale**.
Too eager = lose the speedup; too lazy = serve wrong data.
Tame it with **TTL**, **write-through**, or **explicit invalidation** — each a freshness/speed trade.

quiz.q: What problem does a cache solve?
options: Speed — avoid re-fetching expensive data by keeping a fast local copy
quiz.explain: It turns a slow fetch into an instant local hit.

options: When the source data changes, deciding when to drop the stale copy has no clean universal answer
quiz.explain: Stale copies serve wrong data; over-invalidating kills the speed benefit.

quiz.q: CALLBACK: How does caching connect to Day 2's memory hierarchy?
options: It's the same idea at every level — keep hot data close (CPU cache, RAM, CDN) to dodge the slow tiers
quiz.explain: The memory hierarchy IS caching in hardware; CDNs are caching on the internet. 'Keep the data you need close' all the way up.

tg_quiz.q: The famously 'hard' part of caching is…
options: Invalidation (knowing when the copy is stale)
tg_quiz.correct: Right — cache invalidation, the classic hard problem.
tg_quiz.wrong: It's invalidation — deciding when the cached copy has gone stale.
tg_quiz.explain: Too eager loses speed; too lazy serves wrong data.
